The durable per-server_root_id identity is built from three sticky objects under gc/server-roots/<server_root_id>/: owner (permanent, putIfAbsent once, binds server_root_id to one server_uuid_hex forever), epoch (permanent, CAS-bumped per writable open, a durable monotone writer_epoch counter never reissued), and mount (an expirable heartbeat lease, same-UUID reclaim only after expiry).

server_root_id is a required, validated, immutable config parameter, not derived from ServerUUID; a superseded writer (whose writer_epoch no longer matches the live mount) issues no mutable CAS/PUT because the write-path lease fence is a local in-memory check with no per-write S3 read, tripping the disk to lost/fail-closed on any supersession.

A five-hour CA validation round found an unresolved architecture-level race in CAS pool decommission/owner-retirement: after a mount's owner is deleted and its epoch is already gone, a same-UUID successor can recreate the mount untouched by the owner check, and decommission's delete then removes the live successor's owner anchor; a symmetric owner-token check alone cannot close this because the owner's token never changes on resume, so a fix needs either a symmetric successor-side recheck or a condemn-marker two-phase retirement touching the claim/resume protocol, not just `CasDecommission.cpp`.

`decommissionPoolMember` throws `CORRUPTED_DATA` when a catalog entry is `Removing` but its exact checkpoint (`refCkptKey`) is absent from the backend, refusing to retire the victim slot for that namespace.

`decommissionPoolMember`'s only list-based deletions target three physically loose non-catalog debris prefixes rooted at the victim's own server-root subtree — the manifest sweep, the staging drain (`<pool_prefix>/staging/<victim_srid>/`), and the mountpoint drain (`<pool_prefix>/roots/<victim_srid>/`) — and none of them participates in namespace-ownership selection.

For non-atomic bucket-sync backups, `gc/server-roots/<id>/epoch` (a `WriterEpochMonotoneUnique` durable-monotone counter) can be captured before manifests minted under a later epoch, letting a restored writer re-issue a used `writer_epoch`; the chosen backup design avoids this by never replicating identity objects at all, rather than sequencing the copy to take identity objects last.

`claimOwnerOrThrow` binds `server_root_id` to `server_uuid` permanently via a decision table: an owner present with a `retired_at_ms` tombstone throws `CORRUPTED_DATA` refusing to resume; an owner present with a different uuid throws `CORRUPTED_DATA` naming the regenerated-uuid-file cause and remedies; an absent owner over a non-provably-empty subtree throws `CORRUPTED_DATA` for identity-lost-over-existing-data; and losing the `putIfAbsent` race re-reads, proceeding only if the winning uuid matches. "Provably empty" requires both an authoritative catalog naming no life owned by the srid and 1-key LIST probes finding nothing under `cas/manifests/<srid>/` or `roots/<srid>/`.

A `LOGICAL_ERROR` "release before start" fires when Store teardown calls `stop()`/`doTerminate` on a mount-lease keeper whose `seq` is still 0 because `doStart` threw before completing; this is pure noise during an already-failing shutdown rather than a real defect signal, and the recommended fix is for `doTerminate` with `seq == 0` to be a quiet no-op.

The rev.7/rev.8 disk-lifecycle work landed a `SYSTEM CONTENT ADDRESSED FORGET` verb (with `GC STOP` / `GC START` companions) that unmounts a disk's pool by stopping all background CAS activity (GC, mount-lease renewal) and ejecting the disk, backed by a machine-checked (TLA+ Model 2) lifecycle state machine and an always-present `system.content_addressed_mounts`-style row per pool, rather than the previously-planned natural-erasure proof mechanism.

CAS's single-shard `RootShard` register is linearizable only while single-writer holds, because the shard `casPut` is fenced by a content token, not a monotone `writer_epoch`; a paused/superseded writer (J1), a VM clone sharing `server_uuid` (J2), or wall-clock lease-expiry-vs-boot-clock skew (J3) each open a dual-writer window that produces split-brain / zombie-value / non-linearizable / forked-journal-history anomalies. This is the single headline register-level finding of the Jepsen/Elle-style consistency audit; the fix is to carry `writer_epoch` into the shard-CAS precondition, the same reject-if-stale pattern GC already uses on its `deleteExact`/`gc/state` CAS (which is why GC leadership is already split-brain-safe).

In the CAS mount-fence write-grace plan, no test may `EXPECT_THROW` a `LOGICAL_ERROR`; Part B failure paths must surface as `INVALID_STATE` or `NETWORK_ERROR`, which are safe to assert with `EXPECT_THROW` under sanitizers.

The ack-floor redesign moves the mount-fence deadline to `CLOCK_BOOTTIME` because `CLOCK_MONOTONIC` does not advance during VM suspend.
Each server maintains one merged heartbeat object at `gc/server-roots/<srid>/mount`, replacing the separate `roots/<server-hex>/_watermark` object and `WatermarkKeeper`.

DEFER does not write `gc/state` or advance the round and uses a leader-local in-memory `rounds_since_last_fold`; the lease-renew CAS still runs because it is required to retain leadership and heartbeat liveness.

CAS introspection is read-only and fail-open per row: a corrupt or racing mount body becomes a `state='corrupt'` row or is skipped, never an exception into the query; unlike `computeHeartbeatFloor`, `listMounts` performs no fence writes.

The lease/view decoupling moves S3-heavy retired-view refresh off `MountLeaseKeeper::renewOnce`; renewal reads only cheap in-memory values including `Store::observedGcRound()`, while a Store-owned poller runs `Store::syncRetiredView()` independently.
The mount-lease recovery protocol follows the TLA+ rule that a GC fence costs an epoch: a fenced same-epoch body is never adoptable or refreshable, and recovery always allocates a new writer epoch.

Renewal mismatches are classified by the current mount body: an own fenced body is reported as `fenced_by_gc`, a newer own epoch as superseded, a foreign UUID as a foreign writer, and an unexplained mismatch remains a loud fail-closed exception.

The lease/view implementation splits the merged heartbeat into a cheap renewal path using `Store::observedGcRound()` and a Store-owned `syncRetiredView` poller that performs the S3-heavy work independently.

After `PreconditionFailed` in renewal or adoption, the mount-lease code re-reads the slot body and classifies the refusal by body contents rather than by token alone.

The liveness gate is a token-guarded slot claim on the same path as S13 self-remount: a live member refuses the operation, there is no FORCE variant, and the scope is the whole srid rather than a table.

Rev.6 solves writer exclusivity at the mount-lease boundary and removes the ref protocol's grace machinery; because recovery is lazy per namespace, sealing inside `ensureRefTableRecovered` before exposing table state is equivalent to sealing before writable for `NoDivergentFold`.
CAS ref-writer exclusivity is established at the mount-lease boundary, after which the ref protocol is single-writer by construction.
Wall clocks may be trusted to decline lease acquisition, but lease acquisition and fencing establish liveness by observing token stability on the observer's monotonic clock.
A self-remount waits for unresolved ref-log conditional PUTs to resolve and owes `materialization_grace_ms` only when at least one ref-log PUT remains unresolved.
A `released_clean` marker skips observation, `T_mat`, and the recovery seal on ordinary restarts.
The read-only replica design uses a third CAS mount mode named `reader` that writes only its own `gc/readers/<reader_id>` pin key family and rejects `createTransaction()` with `READONLY`.
`Pool/CasMountRuntime` owns mount fencing, lease keeping, self-remount state, writer epochs, build-sequence watermarks, active builds, `minActive`, and build-sequence allocation/retirement.

The fail-close boundary for renewal is the lease deadline, with `now + lease_safety_margin >= lease_deadline` causing a fence when no successful renewal has refreshed the deadline; a proven supersession still fences immediately.
The renewal fix is confined to `CasServerRoot` and `MountLeaseKeeper`; it does not change generic or upstream ClickHouse code.

`CasMountRuntime` owns mount fencing, the mount lease keeper, self-remount machinery, and build-sequence watermarks, while `CasStore` retains the `open` and `tryRemountOnce` orchestration and its claim→ledger-quiesce→fence-rearm order.

CAS recovery backoff must use `condition_variable::wait_for` tied to the pool shutdown event so pool teardown does not wait out the retry tail.

The rev.8 identity gate compares only `pool_id` and `blob_header_len`; successful decoding is the format gate, while `algos_used` and `min_reader_generation` are refreshed and never compared.

The fence-not-rescue fix has three phases: exhaustive non-aborting classification in `MountLeaseKeeper::onRenewMismatch`, pre-I/O fence-deadline anchoring, and probe-gated writer-epoch re-minting with decommission-aware policy.

The TLA+ model already maps a confirmed renewal mismatch to `localLost` and proves `SupersededWriterMakesNoMutation`; Phase A is therefore an implementation alignment rather than a new model transition.
Both the keeper's wall-clock `confirmed_deadline_ms` and the runtime's boot-clock mutation fence must be anchored at the pre-I/O renewal attempt instant, not at response or acknowledgement time.
The implemented v2 design rejects rescue of ambiguous renewals: a lease holder that cannot confirm its renewal is treated as not live, fenced, and self-remounted with a fresh epoch.

Phase B removes request latency from lease-fence skew by anchoring both deadline domains at attempt start; the keeper uses wall-clock time and the runtime mutation fence uses `CLOCK_BOOTTIME`, so separate anchors are required.

The fence observability work covers both fence-loss modes: throwing renewal followed by self-remount (Mode 1) and silently hanging renewal followed by deadline expiry and late re-arm without remount (Mode 2).
Part B issues no object-store request and cannot make a fence live; only the unchanged self-remount or late renewal path can make `mayMutate()` true.

Write grace complements rather than replaces `CasWriteRetryLater`: after the bound expires or when disabled, plain writes still fail through error 668 and ref-log appends through `NETWORK_ERROR` 210, preserving retry-loop behavior for background writers.

The only remaining whole-round ref abort is a key attributable to no namespace; the mount-claim token-stability observation window remains because a stale-looking lease may belong to a live twin and wall-clock age cannot decide that.

Mount fence recovery treats a `FencedSelf` claim as a typed `MountFencedException`, distinguishes a GC fence of the node's own expired lease from a foreign writer, allocates a fresh `writer_epoch`, and retries the claim in `Store::open`.

Mount lease renewal no longer performs the S3-heavy retired-view refresh; it reads `Store::observedGcRound`, while a dedicated `syncRetiredView` thread advances the view so object-store latency cannot block renewal past the TTL.
The B160 GC lease fix adds an advisory heartbeat register `hb`; a follower steals only when both `(owner, seq)` and `hb` remain frozen throughout its observation window.

`WipeEpoch` models genuine loss of the durable epoch object independently of sabotage flags and is guarded by `epochWiped` so it fires at most once per behavior; repeated loss is outside this gate's scope.
`WatermarkKeeper` and `HeartbeatKeeper` are candidates for a policy-parameterized `SingleWriterSlotKeeper`, but their epoch, farewell, and discard semantics must remain explicit.
The consistency review recommends using `BackgroundSchedulePool` for the periodic CAS GC, heartbeat, and watermark tasks instead of four bespoke periodic thread loops.

The re-triage records that shard-incarnation state carries `writer_epoch`, fencing builds from superseded mount incarnations before they mutate a shard.

Runtime construction follows catalog observation or successful birth, and exact acquisition admits only the observed life and accepted mount-fence generation; an identity conflict returns a typed retry-later outcome instead of rewriting the resident runtime.

The identity/fencing model has three durable layers with a fixed startup order: `OwnerProto`/owner is identity (write-once binding of `server_root_id` to `server_uuid`, clock-free, never deleted or reassigned, foreign UUID fails closed even if a lease is expired); `ServerEpochProto`/epoch is the durable monotone fence (CAS-bumped on each mount attempt, hands out a fresh `writer_epoch`, must survive lease expiry/reclaim, and a missing epoch over non-empty data is a reset hazard); `MountLeaseProto`/mount is liveness (renewed repeatedly, has wall-clock expiry/seq/hostname/pid diagnostics, reclaimable when expired or GC-fenced). Reviewer (Mikhail) disposition on J3 (clock-skew reclaim): the CAS protocol is mostly clock-free already and could be made fully clock-free, but doing so would likely require waiting roughly 30-60 seconds while mounting the disk, and it is not clear that price is a good tradeoff versus keeping the wall-clock lease-expiry mechanism.

`createNamespace` is the only production incarnation mint site, and stale-creator reconciliation changes only `creator` while leaving `state` and `incarnation` unchanged.

Letting tools claim ownership and downgrading failures afterward is rejected because a tool can claim a fresh empty pool under uuid `0000…`, burn a durable writer epoch before refusal, and join the GC heartbeat ack floor.

The decommission owner-anchor tombstone race remains deferred: a same-UUID successor can be recreated between the liveness recheck and owner CAS, and the operational rule is not to run `DROP POOL MEMBER` while the victim may be restarting.

Rejected-birth checkpoint cleanup must be bound to the exact object version created by the attempt and to a catalog state or fence proving exclusive ownership; otherwise the cleanup must retain responsibility.

Per-part write-time files uuid.txt, txn_version.txt, and metadata_version.txt are ordinary PartManifest entries, not a separate mutable sidecar; a single-file change on an already-committed part resolves through a committed-ref repoint that carries every unchanged entry forward and republishes one manifest, and a byte-identical rewrite is a zero-pool-mutation no-op (repointRef).

A SQL DROP PART/DROP PARTITION is modeled as removal supersession: an additive commit creates a real part ref, a removal creates an empty covering tombstone ref promoted from MergeTreeData::dropPartImpl's local Outdated empty covering part into a persisted, Active, covering ref using the existing ActiveDataPartSet/getActiveContainingPart covering machinery. This persisted part ref is distinct from the D1 shard-object tombstone, which is a journal marker letting GC reclaim an empty shard object.

DROP PART has a documented weak guarantee under a mid-range race with a concurrent merge: the merge may produce a real covering part carrying the data, so DROP PART can end up merged into a bigger part instead of deleting it (ReplicatedMergeTreeLogEntryData::getVirtualPartNames returns {} for DROP_PART). The persisted tombstone for a mid-range single part is therefore conditional/reconciled, not unconditional: if a real covering part wins the race, the tombstone must not strand or double-cover.

FREEZE must materialize real bytes into the local shadow/ directory and cannot be reference-only, because shadow/'s documented contract is filesystem-readable hardlinks consumed by external backup pipelines; freeze/freezeRemote/clonePart are independent IDataPartStorage virtuals not built on createHardLinkFrom. A self-describing snapshots/<name> ref-set may exist as an additional in-pool reachability root for restore-by-reference but does not replace byte materialization.

Since the all-tree part-files migration, filling in the creation CSN on COMMIT and locking/unlocking the removal TID on an already-committed part are ordinary committed-ref standalone writes through `repointRef`, not a special mutable-only case: every OTHER committed manifest entry is carried forward and a byte-identical rewrite resolves through `repointRef`'s byte-equal check with zero pool mutations.

An uncommitted INSERT inside an open transaction still publishes a CAS ref whose blobs stay GC-reachable via a `WriteSession` pin until the ref lands; the part is logically invisible via its `txn_version.txt` creation CSN. ROLLBACK removes the ref, after which the blobs become GC-eligible.

A transactional merge/mutation spanning multiple parts is keyed by a per-part staging map, `parts: (namespace, ref) -> PartStaging`, rather than a single `(table_uuid, part_name)`; a deferred rename (`tmp_merge_X -> X`) moves the staging entry to the destination key and merges it with any destination entry a deferred-window `txn_version.txt` write already created. `commit` takes the `gc_lock` once and iterates `parts`, applying the whole-part publish or the mutable-only branch per entry.

A transactional multi-part commit is not filesystem-atomic on CAS: MVCC visibility is gated by the per-part CSN/TID in `txn_version.txt`, not by disk-op atomicity, so CAS may publish parts one at a time; a crash mid-commit leaves some refs published and some not, and orphan refs are GC-reclaimed exactly as any uncommitted-then-abandoned build (B122).

CAS refuses BACKUP via temporary hard links for Ordinary (non-UUID) databases with `SUPPORT_IS_DISABLED`, while Atomic databases back up normally; partition commands are refused outside an explicit allowlist (DROP_PARTITION, DROP_DETACHED_PARTITION, FORGET_PARTITION, ATTACH_PARTITION, REPLACE_PARTITION, MOVE_PARTITION, FETCH_PARTITION, FREEZE_*, UNFREEZE_*); `supportsChmod`/`supportsStat` are false and `getHardlinkCount` returns 0; bucket versioning must not be enabled and is probed and refused; and `<readonly>1</readonly>` disks take no mount claim, run no probe, no writes, and no GC.

The writer no longer synchronizes a retired view or writer-side ack floor; it point-reads an add-only freshness meta at promote and copy-forward.

The two-level write API puts terminal committed-ref primitives and `republishRef` in the facade, while `publishEntries` replaces the near-duplicate publish body of `adoptPartFromManifest` and transaction staging remains in the transaction.
Writer cleanup removes stale precommit ownership, and weak fairness of successor maintenance is expected to eventually clean pending stale ownership.
Dead-precommit removal moved from GC to the writer, which appends exact `owner_transition` removals; GC reclaims the resulting blobs through ordinary edge cancellation.

Pool-member decommission performs full srid erasure of namespaces, manifest debris, staging, roots objects, and the slot, while subsequent normal GC rounds reclaim the now-unreferenced blob bytes.
On atomic-write storages, `VersionMetadataOnDisk` writes version information with one `writeFile` instead of a temporary file plus rename.

`Pool/CasBlobUploader` moves byte-delivery execution out of `CasBuild`, while admit/adopt/resurrect decisions and dependency-set recording remain on the transaction class.
The proposed MOVE-to-CA fix is a CAS-aware `clonePart` path that stages the whole part in one `ContentAddressedTransaction`; the generic per-file cross-disk copy path is insufficient.
Whole-part atomicity sites such as `freeze`, restore-from-backup, and B58 projection commits remain single-`commit` transactions because this design deliberately introduces no `precommit` phase.

Verbatim table-level and mountpoint files are treated as an immediate autocommit class: writes are durable on finalize and deletes or moves remain durable at call time, avoiding a second timeline for those files.

The MOVE-to-CA design was reframed as one whole-part `ContentAddressedTransaction` threaded through the move, plus a layer-1 parser fix so the final part identity is used instead of `moving`; the earlier claim that a transactional copy would lack full build semantics was rejected.

Review finding №12's call-time mutation of durable refs is by design: `renameParts` is the commit point and rollback compensates with new operations over committed disk state, but `removeDirectory` must discard staged entries when removing a part before commit.
The generic fix closes every part disk-storage transaction in `MergeTreeData::Transaction::renameParts` after deferred renames, with no CA-specific code change.

The intended protocol is prepare durable and compensable storage before the Keeper decision, then apply visibility with a cheap finalize or compensate on abort; `renameParts` is the existing lock-free prepare slot.

The agreed fix model closes the disk transaction at `renameParts`; a later parts-transaction commit has nothing left to do on disk, while rollback performs compensation as a new operation over committed state.

For CA part moves, the crash-atomic design uses a transient `moving/<part>` reference prefix: `clonePart` commits under the moving reference and the mover later repoints it to the final reference, so startup cleanup can reclaim an orphaned moving reference.

The production INSERT topology commits one `ContentAddressedTransaction` per part, so cross-part batching must occur at the `MergeTreeData::Transaction::renameParts` seam rather than inside `ContentAddressedTransaction::commit`.

The phased engine uses one precommit ledger batch, one flattened cross-part upload wave, and one promote ledger batch; a 500-part INSERT is expected to reduce about 1026 serial ref-log PUTs to about two.

A plain INSERT performs one `ContentAddressedTransaction::commit()` per part with `parts.size() == 1`, so inner-loop parallelism cannot improve INSERT; cross-part concurrency must be introduced above the disk transaction.

The approved inner-loop design dispatches each part's unchanged `stageManifest → precommitAdd → uploadPendingBlobs → promote` sequence to bounded workers, preserving per-part ordering while overlapping parts.

The CAS commit pool must use bounded worker-loop callbacks or a dedicated pool sized by `cas_commit_concurrency`; scheduling one task per part on a shared 100-thread pool would not enforce the bound and could starve unrelated users.

The initial multi-commit design used `commitTransactions` as a transaction-centric seam: generic implementations loop sequentially, while `MergeTreeData::Transaction::renameParts` groups same-disk transactions without leaking `isContentAddressed` checks into generic MergeTree code.
`PreparedPartWrite` makes the receiver's durable `+1` and deferred promote an owned state: callers must explicitly `promote` or `abort`, because destruction of the handle alone is not cleanup.

Move assignment for `PreparedPartWrite` is deleted because overwriting a handle that still owes a terminal action may require a fallible `abandon`, which move assignment cannot report without dropping cleanup ownership.

The part-write release seam is relink-independent: any `PartWriteTxn` may leave a staged precommit whose release is unproven, and the accounting is intentionally not attributed to relink or another consumer.

`~PartWriteTxn`, rather than `~PreparedPartWrite`, owns the final release word because `prepareEntries` can fail before constructing a handle; the transaction destructor therefore covers both handle and no-handle staging exits.

`Poisoned` is not equivalent to a wedge: it means a durable transaction may be missing from the cached view, so it continues to block snapshot publication and triggers re-recovery; making `ApplyPending` debug-only is a follow-up, not part of Stage B.

The `RemovalReady` protocol is adopted as a transient catalog state between `Removing` and entry deletion: it is entered only after the terminal record has folded and the life-scoped cleanup item is durably `Completed`.

The final recommendation is to keep `NamespaceLifeId` and incarnation-qualified ref and namespace-file keys, avoid permanent `Retired` history and extra retirement markers, and delete a catalog entry only after terminal fold, cleanup/cursor retirement, and exact `_ckpt` deletion ordering is complete.

The incarnation is retained because temporary refusal alone cannot make omitted old physical objects safe for eventual same-name reuse; the generation makes old ref objects and namespace files structurally inert.

The `RemovalReady` state machine is `Creating -> Live -> Removing -> RemovalReady -> absent`; `RemovalReady` means no writer publication, recovery, ref fold, or new cursor is permitted, and only exact removal of the row is legal.

Physical `_files` debris is outside namespace rebirth gating; incomplete `LIST` may defer reclamation and leak bytes, but cannot expose an old file through a new life or prevent the new life from being admitted.

`Build::abandon` must call `retireBuildSeq` only after the precommit-removal `mutateShard`, so the build becomes watermark-dead only after its removal is durable; this ordering mirrors `Build::promote`.

The tokenless DETACH/freeze adopt path can race GC condemnation because `copyForwardFromCondemned` runs once before the CAS closure; the proposed fix is a bounded copy-forward and re-HEAD loop outside the closure, analogous to tokened resurrection.
